Transformer-Based Reinforcement Learning for Phase I Dose Allocation

Shijie Yuan Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin Email: sj.yuan@austin.utexas.edu
Abstract

Phase I dose-finding trials must learn from sparse toxicity observations while limiting exposure to overly toxic doses. We develop a single reinforcement-learning policy for trials with different numbers of ordered dose levels. Each dose is represented as a token containing its normalized position, accumulated patient count, observed dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs), and current-dose indicator. A Transformer encoder summarizes the dose tokens, trial-conditioned cross-attention produces a fixed-dimensional trial representation, and a three-action policy chooses de-escalation, staying, or escalation. The final maximum tolerated dose (MTD) decision is deliberately kept outside the learned policy: after the planned sample size, weighted isotonic regression and a prespecified safety cap select the dose closest to the target toxicity probability. In the simulations, toxicity-penalized policies reduce DLT burden while unpenalized policies improve selection accuracy at the cost of greater toxicity. These results demonstrate a controllable safety–accuracy trade-off but do not establish superiority over conventional dose-finding designs.

1 Introduction

Phase I oncology trials must learn an acceptable dose from limited patient cohorts while protecting participants from excessive toxicity. The operational decision is sequential: after each cohort, the trial must decide whether to escalate, remain at the current dose, or de-escalate. The statistical target is usually expressed through a dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) probability ϕ\phi, but the evidence available at each decision is sparse and unevenly distributed across dose levels.

For example, consider a trial with six ordered dose levels, d1<⋯<d6d_{1}<\cdots<d_{6}, and a target DLT probability of ϕ=0.25\phi=0.25. The trial may begin at d1d_{1} and observe no DLTs in the first cohort, supporting escalation to d2d_{2}. If subsequent cohorts at d2d_{2} and d3d_{3} continue to show little toxicity, the allocation rule may move upward to gather information near the target. Conversely, if two DLTs are observed among three patients at d3d_{3}, the next decision should become more conservative: the trial may remain at d3d_{3}, de-escalate to d2d_{2}, or stop if the evidence indicates that even the lowest dose is unsafe. The same observed DLT count can imply different actions depending on the current dose, the number of patients already treated, the remaining sample-size budget, and the information collected at neighboring doses. This context dependence is the central sequential-allocation problem addressed here.

Conventional Phase I designs provide important safety and interpretability properties. Algorithmic and model-assisted approaches such as BOIN, i3+3, and mTPI-2 use prespecified decision boundaries or interval-based rules (Liu and Yuan,, 2015; Liu et al.,, 2020; Guo et al.,, 2017). Model-based approaches such as CRM impose a dose–toxicity model (O’Quigley et al.,, 1990; Cheung,, 2011), while isotonic approaches provide an alternative way to enforce monotonicity when estimating a dose close to the target (Ivanova and Flournoy,, 2009). These conventional dose-finding designs are strong reference methods, but their allocation rules are generally specified for a fixed dose grid and do not learn a shared representation across trials with different numbers of dose levels.

Deep reinforcement learning has recently been explored for Phase I dose escalation (Matsuura et al.,, 2023), creating an opportunity to optimize sequential allocation directly against trial-level objectives. In the reported formulation, the escalation rule is learned through simulated trials, as is typical for model development in this setting. Consequently, its operating characteristics are tied to the prespecified state, action, reward, and scenario-generating distributions, and the extent to which the learned rule transfers to alternative dose grids or clinical settings remains an empirical question. The multidimensional policy may also require additional tools for interpretation, and coupling allocation with final MTD recommendation can make it less direct to separate sequential-allocation error from final-dose-estimation error.

These considerations motivate a framework with a shared representation across variable numbers of dose levels and an explicitly prespecified final selection rule. The proposed approach retains the flexibility of learned sequential allocation while keeping the final clinical recommendation transparent and separately evaluable.

The challenge is to obtain the flexibility of a learned policy without sacrificing transparency or allowing a training reward to define the final clinical recommendation implicitly. We therefore separate allocation from final selection. During the trial, a policy learns only the next-cohort action. At planned completion, a prespecified weighted isotonic-regression rule selects the MTD from observed data. This separation also makes safety–accuracy trade-offs visible: a policy can be evaluated by DLT burden, incorrect early stopping, and MTD-selection accuracy rather than by a single reward alone.

We present a Transformer-based reinforcement-learning framework in which dose levels are represented as a variable-length token sequence and trial-level context supplies a query for cross-attention. The resulting representation supports a fixed three-action policy for trials with different dose counts. The study asks whether this representation can improve sequential allocation while retaining a transparent final selector, and how the answer changes when the reward penalizes DLTs.

This paper makes three contributions. First, it formulates variable-dose Phase I allocation as a trial-conditioned representation-learning problem with a fixed action space. Second, it evaluates the resulting policy under a prespecified final MTD-selection rule and matched benchmark designs. Third, it characterizes the resulting safety–accuracy trade-off across dose counts, reward penalties, learning rates, and random seeds. Taken together, these contributions provide an empirical framework for studying flexible allocation under explicit safety criteria, rather than a claim that the current policy dominates conventional dose-finding designs.

2 Methods

Each simulated trial is treated as one episode. First, the simulator samples a monotone dose–toxicity curve and trial-level design parameters. Patients are then treated in cohorts, and the resulting DLT outcomes update the observed counts at the current dose. At each decision point, the Transformer converts the dose-level observations and trial context into a fixed-dimensional representation; the policy uses this representation to choose de-escalation, staying, or escalation subject to boundary masks. The episode ends either at an early safety boundary or when the maximum sample size is reached. Only in the latter case does a prespecified weighted isotonic-regression rule select the final MTD. This workflow separates the learned sequential allocation problem from the final statistical recommendation and provides the structure for the technical components below.

2.1 Sequential dose-allocation framework

Consider ordered dose levels d1<⋯<dJd_{1}<\cdots<d_{J}, target DLT probability ϕ\phi, and maximum sample size NmaxN_{\max}. At decision time tt, dose jj is represented by

zj,t=(d¯j,nj,t,xj,t,𝕀{j=jt}),d¯j=j−1J−1,z_{j,t}=\left(\bar{d}_{j},n_{j,t},x_{j,t},\mathbb{I}\{j=j_{t}\}\right),\qquad\bar{d}_{j}=\frac{j-1}{J-1}, (1)

where nj,tn_{j,t} and xj,tx_{j,t} are the observed patient and DLT counts. The trial query is

ct=(ϕ,Nmax,nt,d¯jt,J,b),c_{t}=\left(\phi,N_{\max},n_{t},\bar{d}_{j_{t}},J,b\right), (2)

with bb the planned cohort size. The policy observes these quantities but not the simulated truth, including the underlying toxicity curve or true MTD.

The dose tokens pass through a shared Transformer encoder, following the self-attention architecture introduced for sequence representation learning (Vaswani et al.,, 2017). A query derived from ctc_{t} attends over the encoded dose tokens, yielding a fixed-dimensional representation independent of JJ. The use of shared token processing and aggregation is also related to variable-cardinality representations such as Deep Sets (Zaheer et al.,, 2017); unlike a permutation-invariant set representation, the present model retains dose order through the normalized dose-position feature. A policy head outputs three actions:

𝒜={−1,0,+1}={de-escalate,stay,escalate}.\mathcal{A}=\{-1,0,+1\}=\{\text{de-escalate},\text{stay},\text{escalate}\}. (3)

At the highest dose, escalation is masked. At the lowest dose, de-escalation remains available and means early safety stopping with no dose recommended. This boundary action is operationally useful but is not itself a statistical proof that every dose is unsafe.

Each episode begins at j0=1j_{0}=1. After a cohort is treated, the simulator generates individual outcomes

Yt,r∼Bernoulli(pjt),r=1,…,bt,Y_{t,r}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{j_{t}}),\qquad r=1,\ldots,b_{t}, (4)

where bt=min⁡{b,Nmax−nt}b_{t}=\min\{b,N_{\max}-n_{t}\} allows the final cohort to be smaller than the planned cohort. If Xt=∑rYt,rX_{t}=\sum_{r}Y_{t,r} denotes the cohort DLT count, the observed state is updated by

njt,t+1=njt,t+bt,xjt,t+1=xjt,t+Xt.n_{j_{t},t+1}=n_{j_{t},t}+b_{t},\qquad x_{j_{t},t+1}=x_{j_{t},t}+X_{t}. (5)

The policy is queried only after the cohort outcomes are available. Thus, the simulator may retain the true curve for evaluation and reward calculation, but the policy receives no information about pjp_{j}, the true MTD, future outcomes, or the scenario label.

The action mask is applied before sampling from the policy distribution. De-escalation at the lowest dose is deliberately not masked because it is the model’s explicit early-stop mechanism; escalation at the highest dose is masked because it would leave the dose grid. These rules yield at most 2​J−12J-1 policy decisions when Nmax=6​JN_{\max}=6J and b=3b=3, because the last cohort is followed directly by final selection.

2.2 Trial-conditioned cross-attention

As summarized in Figure 1, the cross-attention layer converts a variable-length collection of dose representations into one trial representation. Attention was originally introduced as a learned soft alignment between a query state and relevant elements of an encoded sequence (Bahdanau et al.,, 2015); later work formalized global and local attention variants (Luong et al.,, 2015). In the proposed framework, the dose sequence supplies the information to be retrieved, while the trial query specifies what information is relevant for the current decision.

Let Ht∈ℝJ×pH_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times p} denote the encoded dose tokens and let qt∈ℝpq_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} denote the embedded trial context. Cross-attention produces a fixed-dimensional trial representation

htrial,t=MHA⁡(qt,Ht,Ht,Mt),h_{\mathrm{trial},t}=\operatorname{MHA}\!\left(q_{t},H_{t},H_{t};\,M_{t}\right), (6)

where the trial context supplies the query and the dose representations supply the keys and values. The mask MtM_{t} excludes padding positions, so the representation is valid for any number of dose levels. The implementation uses four heads and model dimension p=64p=64; the policy and value heads therefore receive the same-sized input for every JJ.

The purpose of this layer is selective retrieval. For illustration, the architecture can represent a decision that emphasizes the current dose and nearby toxicity observations early in a trial, or one that emphasizes more extensively studied doses and evidence near the target later in a trial. These examples describe the types of state-dependent weighting that cross-attention can express; they are not claims about the attention patterns necessarily learned by the fitted policy. Unlike masked mean pooling, which gives every observed dose the same aggregation weight, cross-attention can adapt its weights to the current state. The weights are learned for action prediction and are not posterior probabilities that a dose is the MTD. Standard query/key/value projections, scaling, and multi-head concatenation are given in Appendix A; the main text focuses on why the mechanism is useful for variable-dose trials.

2.3 Prespecified final MTD selection

If a trial reaches NmaxN_{\max}, the implementation computes empirical toxicity rates for tried doses and fits weighted isotonic regression, enforcing the expected monotonicity of toxicity with dose (Barlow and Brunk,, 1972; Ivanova and Flournoy,, 2009):

(p~j)j∈𝒪=arg⁡min⁡∑j∈𝒪qj​nondecreasing⁡nj​(qj−p^j)2.(\widetilde{p}_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{O}}=\arg\min_{q_{j}\ \mathrm{nondecreasing}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{O}}n_{j}(q_{j}-\widehat{p}_{j})^{2}. (7)

Only doses with p~j≤ϕ+0.05\widetilde{p}_{j}\leq\phi+0.05 are eligible. Among eligible tried doses, the recommendation minimizes |p~j−ϕ||\widetilde{p}_{j}-\phi|. Ties within an isotonic block are resolved toward the highest dose when the fitted value is at or below ϕ\phi, and toward the lowest dose when it is above ϕ\phi. If no dose is eligible, the outcome is no recommendation.

An analysis of the terminal selection procedure indicated that the approximately 0.100.10 improvement in PCS was primarily attributable to the revised tie-breaking rule rather than the safety cap. Therefore, primary comparisons use the common v2 selection rule where stated.

2.4 Simulation and training protocol

The simulation uses monotone dose–toxicity curves with J∈{4,6,8,10}J\in\{4,6,8,10\}, target ϕ∈{0.25,0.30}\phi\in\{0.25,0.30\}, cohort size b=3b=3, and Nmax=6​JN_{\max}=6J. The primary curves are generated from

pj=logit−1⁡(α+β​j−1J−1),β>0,p_{j}=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\left(\alpha+\beta\frac{j-1}{J-1}\right),\qquad\beta>0, (8)

with parameters varied to produce low-toxicity, target-centered, high-toxicity, plateau, and steep scenarios. The simulation design also includes monotone nonparametric curves generated from positive random increments as a stress test of reliance on one logistic functional form. A dose is acceptable when pj≤ϕsafep_{j}\leq\phi_{\mathrm{safe}}; the primary setting uses ϕsafe=ϕ\phi_{\mathrm{safe}}=\phi. The true MTD is the acceptable dose closest to ϕ\phi, with the lowest index used to resolve ties. For the 10% no-dose scenarios, the DLT probability at the lowest dose satisfies p1>ϕsafe+δp_{1}>\phi_{\mathrm{safe}}+\delta with δ=0.05\delta=0.05, which guarantees that all doses are unsafe while avoiding ambiguous cases immediately adjacent to the safety boundary.

Each DLT contributes an immediate penalty −λDLT-\lambda_{\mathrm{DLT}}. The terminal outcome receives +1+1 for correct MTD selection or correct no-dose classification and −1-1 for an incorrect recommendation. Early stopping at the lowest dose receives +1+1 in a no-dose scenario and −1-1 when an acceptable dose exists. Consequently, the episode reward can be written as

R=Rterminal−λDLT​DT,R=R_{\mathrm{terminal}}-\lambda_{\mathrm{DLT}}D_{T}, (9)

where DTD_{T} is the total number of observed DLTs. For an early-terminated episode, RterminalR_{\mathrm{terminal}} is replaced by Rearly​stopR_{\mathrm{early\,stop}}. The primary penalty is λDLT=0.05\lambda_{\mathrm{DLT}}=0.05; λDLT=0\lambda_{\mathrm{DLT}}=0 is evaluated as a sensitivity analysis. This decomposition is important because the scalar reward is an optimization target, whereas PCS, no-dose accuracy, false stopping, and DLT burden are the clinical operating characteristics.

The main PPO configuration uses a two-layer, four-head Transformer with model dimension 64, four PPO epochs, generalized advantage estimation parameter 0.950.95, discount factor γ=1\gamma=1, entropy coefficient 0.010.01, and batches of 256 simulated trials. PPO is used because it provides a practical policy-gradient optimization procedure for the episodic allocation problem (Schulman et al.,, 2017). Training consists of 300 stage-one iterations followed by 3000 stage-two iterations in the long runs. The value network is trained jointly with the policy; the final isotonic selector is not learned. Padding masks are kept fixed across batches containing different values of JJ, and the same action mask is used when computing both action probabilities and log probabilities.

The simulation separates training, validation, and testing by random seed. Validation scenarios are used for optimization monitoring and training decisions, while the final evaluation uses 5000 independent same-distribution test scenarios and greedy policies. The primary analysis reports means and standard deviations across five RL seeds; optimization-sweep analyses use three seeds. Benchmark designs include BOIN, i3+3, mTPI-2, and CRM (Liu and Yuan,, 2015; Liu et al.,, 2020; Guo et al.,, 2017; O’Quigley et al.,, 1990). Because each benchmark design has its own toxicity-elimination and final-selection rules, the primary comparison reports both their original operating characteristics and, where stated, matched evaluations using the common isotonic selector. This distinction prevents final-selection differences from being attributed incorrectly to the sequential allocation policy.

The primary test distribution is not intended to establish extrapolation to unseen dose counts. A planned external-validity analysis would freeze the trained policy and evaluate it on dose counts such as J=5,7,9J=5,7,9, shifted target probabilities, altered sample sizes, delayed outcomes, and non-logistic curves. These settings are therefore treated as generalization targets rather than pooled with the current primary estimates.

2.5 Operating characteristics and comparator interpretation

The primary endpoint is the probability of correct selection (PCS), where a no-dose outcome is correct when no acceptable dose exists. We additionally record the probability that the true MTD was ever tried, PCS conditional on the true MTD being tried, correct no-dose probability, erroneous early stopping, mean DLT count, DLT proportion, the fraction of patients assigned above ϕsafe\phi_{\mathrm{safe}}, and the distribution of patients across dose levels. For scenarios with a true MTD, we report POS, the probability that the selected dose exceeds the true MTD; PCA, the proportion of patients allocated at the true MTD; and POA, the proportion of patients allocated above the true MTD. These three allocation and selection metrics are undefined in no-dose scenarios and are therefore averaged only over scenarios with an acceptable dose. The conditional PCS diagnostic is necessary because a final selector cannot recommend an untried true MTD. Unconditional PCS therefore combines an allocation problem with a final-estimation problem.

The benchmark designs are simulated under the same dose grids, cohort size, starting dose, sample-size budget, and scenario draws. Their original implementations include toxicity-elimination rules, whereas the primary RL policy uses only its learned boundary stop. In addition, CRM can move more than one dose level in a single update, while the RL policy and the interval-based benchmark designs move at most one level. These differences are retained in the primary benchmark because they reflect the complete operating procedures of the methods. Matched final-selection analyses are used as secondary diagnostics to isolate the effect of the sequential allocation component.

3 Results

3.1 Safety–accuracy trade-off under toxicity penalties

We first compared the toxicity-penalized RL policy with the benchmark designs under a common v2 final-selection rule. This experiment tests the primary clinical trade-off: whether reducing DLT exposure is accompanied by an unacceptable loss of MTD-selection accuracy.

The toxicity-penalized policies have lower POS and POA than the benchmark designs, indicating fewer selections and allocations above the true MTD, while PCA is also lower. Thus, the safety benefit is expressed not only through aggregate DLT burden but also through more conservative allocation relative to the true target. The total reward is highest for the penalized RL policies in this comparison because the reward explicitly values reduced toxicity; it should not be interpreted as a universal clinical performance metric.

The dose-stratified curves indicate that the safety benefit is not uniform across trial sizes: as JJ increases, the penalized policy becomes increasingly conservative relative to the comparators. This pattern suggests that dose-grid size remains an important determinant of policy behavior.

3.2 Behavioral effect of the DLT penalty

We next removed the DLT penalty while holding the principal simulation and evaluation protocol fixed. This isolates whether the safety–accuracy pattern is caused by the architecture or by the objective used to train it. Removing the DLT penalty improves selection accuracy but increases toxicity. The two no-penalty settings reach PCS values of 0.5950.595 and 0.6050.605, comparable to or slightly above the benchmark values, while mean DLTs increase to approximately 9.1–9.8 and the unsafe-patient fraction increases to approximately 0.32–0.36. False-stop rates are lower without the penalty, at 0.0040.004–0.0080.008.

The no-penalty curves indicate that improved selection accuracy is achieved through more aggressive exploration, particularly in larger dose grids. Because the final selection rule is fixed, this pattern is attributable to allocation behavior rather than to the selector.

3.3 Performance across dose-grid sizes

To test the variable-length representation, we examined operating characteristics separately for J=4,6,8,10J=4,6,8,10. Figures 2 and 3 show that the policy remains operational across all four dose counts, but performance is not invariant to JJ. Under the DLT penalty, PCS declines as the number of dose levels increases, and the RL policies remain below the rule-based reference lines at J=8J=8 and J=10J=10. Without the penalty, this increase in difficulty as JJ grows is accompanied by higher DLT burden and a higher probability of treating above the MTD. The variable-length architecture therefore enables deployment across dose counts, but does not by itself eliminate dose-count-dependent performance differences.

The training curves show substantial seed-dependent trajectories and no common late-stage improvement, supporting interpretation of the final policy as a stochastic optimization outcome.

3.4 Training stability across learning rates and seeds

We then assessed whether the observed operating characteristics were stable across optimization trajectories. Figure 4 shows the validation PCS and mean DLT trajectories for the two five-seed learning-rate settings with λDLT=0.05\lambda_{\mathrm{DLT}}=0.05. The logged plateau analysis found no significant late-stage trend in training return or validation PCS for the five-seed long runs. The 10−410^{-4} setting generally plateaued after roughly 500–1000 stage-two iterations, while 3×10−53\times 10^{-5} plateaued later, around 1500–2000 iterations. Seed variability is material: for the toxicity-penalized 10−410^{-4} setting, the observed PCS range across seeds was approximately 0.538–0.581, larger than the estimated test-set sampling error. The learning-rate comparison therefore does not establish a clear winner; it primarily demonstrates that seed variation is large enough to require multi-seed reporting.

3.5 Robustness to PPO optimization settings

Finally, we examined the completed three-seed sweep over batch size and entropy coefficient. This analysis asks whether the variability observed above can be reduced through commonly tuned PPO settings. The sweep is interpreted within the RL conditions; its benchmark rows used their original final-selection rules and are therefore not pooled with the primary shared-selection comparison.

The sweep does not identify a universally best optimizer setting. The trajectories and final summaries together suggest that batch size and entropy affect the balance between convergence stability, safety, and selection accuracy, so optimization sensitivity should be reported as a robustness analysis rather than reduced to a single reward-maximizing configuration. With a DLT penalty, batch 1024 lowers DLT burden but also lowers PCS and increases false stopping; without the penalty, it slightly improves PCS while increasing DLT exposure.

3.6 Separating allocation and final-selection error

Overall PCS combines at least two processes: whether the sequential policy ever tries the true MTD, and whether the final selector chooses it after it has been tried. The aggregate evaluation reports PCS, false-stop rate, DLT burden, and unsafe-patient fraction, but does not yet report PCS conditional on trying the true MTD. This distinction is important because an untried true MTD is necessarily unavailable to the isotonic final selector. The present results therefore establish a combined operating characteristic, not a complete attribution of selection error. A full diagnostic analysis should report the probability that the true MTD was tried, conditional PCS given that event, correct no-dose probability, and erroneous early-stop probability.

3.7 Summary of empirical findings

Taken together, the experiments show that the policy’s operating characteristics depend materially on the reward penalty, dose-grid size, and optimization seed. The results motivate the more detailed interpretation and limitations discussed below rather than supporting a claim of uniform superiority over the benchmark designs.

4 Discussion

4.1 Interpretation of findings

The principal finding is a controllable trade-off rather than uniform superiority. Penalizing DLTs led the policy to expose fewer patients to toxicity, but reduced PCS relative to the benchmark designs. Removing that penalty moved PCS into the benchmark range while increasing DLT burden and unsafe-patient allocation. This pattern is consistent with the reward definition: the policy is optimizing a different objective when toxicity carries an immediate cost.

The results also show why the final selector should remain explicit. The isotonic rule and its tie-breaking convention materially affect PCS, and the current aggregate PCS combines sequential exploration with final-dose estimation. Keeping this stage prespecified makes the source of the trade-off more inspectable, but it also means that improvements in the learned allocation policy cannot be inferred from PCS alone.

4.2 Practical implications

The framework is best viewed as a simulation platform for evaluating safety-constrained allocation policies. In a practical development program, PCS, correct no-dose decisions, false-stop probability, mean DLTs, and the fraction of patients assigned above the MTD should be reported jointly. A scalar episode reward is useful for optimization but is not sufficient for clinical interpretation.

The variable-length representation is potentially useful when a development program evaluates related dose grids or when the number of doses differs across protocols. The dose-count stratification nevertheless shows that parameter sharing does not guarantee equal performance across JJ. Practical deployment would also require prespecified operating-characteristic thresholds and trial-design software and workflow support (Zhou et al.,, 2021). The toxicity penalty is a soft safety constraint rather than a formal guarantee; safe reinforcement-learning methods and constrained policy-optimization approaches provide relevant methodological directions (García and Fernández,, 2015; Achiam et al.,, 2017).

4.3 Limitations

The study is simulation-based and currently evaluates same-distribution test scenarios. Logistic monotone curves may not capture all clinically relevant dose–toxicity shapes, and pending outcomes are not modeled. Time-to-event extensions such as TITE-BOIN explicitly address late-onset toxicity and incomplete follow-up (Yuan et al.,, 2018; Chen et al.,, 2025); adapting the present RL environment to those settings is an important limitation and future extension. The RL policy does not yet use an independent overdose-protection rule or a statistical toxicity-elimination rule, whereas the benchmark designs include their own safety mechanisms. The reported benchmark-design values are single simulation runs, whereas RL values average over seeds; the comparison is therefore informative but not perfectly symmetric. The completed optimization sweep uses three seeds and a different comparator-selection convention from the primary analysis.

4.4 Future work

Future simulation studies should evaluate non-logistic and shifted scenario families, unseen dose counts, multiple independent replicates for every benchmark design, and the allocation/final-selection decomposition of PCS. Probability-of-decision designs offer another strategy for accelerating Phase I decisions and could inform future extensions of the allocation environment (Zhou et al.,, 2020). A clinically richer extension could add pharmacokinetic and pharmacometric information to the trial context and dose tokens, building on recent pharmacometrics-enabled dose-optimization work for seamless Phase I–II oncology trials (Yuan et al.,, 2026). Another extension could allow backfill enrollment, so that patients can be assigned to previously explored lower doses while escalation continues, as in the backfill i3+3 design (Liu et al.,, 2023). These additions would require explicit modeling of information availability, cohort timing, and the safety rules governing concurrent dose assignments. Additional ablations should isolate the Transformer encoder, cross-attention, and variable-dose training. Finally, the DLT penalty should be calibrated against an explicitly stated safety or utility criterion rather than selected solely by total episode reward.

In conclusion, this study presents a variable-length Transformer reinforcement-learning framework for sequential Phase I dose allocation with trial-conditioned cross-attention and a transparent, prespecified final MTD selector. The simulations show that toxicity penalties reduce DLT exposure but trade away some selection accuracy, whereas removing the penalty produces more accurate but more aggressive allocation. The framework provides a structured platform for evaluating safety-constrained policies against benchmark designs and for future extensions incorporating richer clinical information.

Appendix A Standard cross-attention details

For completeness, the multi-head cross-attention used in the policy is specified here. For head mm, the embedded trial query and encoded dose tokens are projected as

Qt(m)=qt​WQ(m),Kt(m)=Ht​WK(m),Vt(m)=Ht​WV(m).Q_{t}^{(m)}=q_{t}W_{Q}^{(m)},\qquad K_{t}^{(m)}=H_{t}W_{K}^{(m)},\qquad V_{t}^{(m)}=H_{t}W_{V}^{(m)}. (10)

The attention weights are

αt(m)=softmax⁡(Qt(m)​Kt(m)⊤dk+Mt),\alpha_{t}^{(m)}=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{Q_{t}^{(m)}K_{t}^{(m)\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}+M_{t}\right), (11)

where MtM_{t} assigns a large negative value to padded dose positions. The head output is ut(m)=αt(m)​Vt(m)u_{t}^{(m)}=\alpha_{t}^{(m)}V_{t}^{(m)}, and the multi-head output is

htrial,t=Concat⁡(ut(1),…,ut(M))​WO.h_{\mathrm{trial},t}=\operatorname{Concat}\left(u_{t}^{(1)},\ldots,u_{t}^{(M)}\right)W_{O}. (12)

The implementation uses four heads, model dimension p=64p=64, and a shared encoder across dose counts. The no-cross-attention ablation replaces this operation with masked mean pooling of the encoded dose tokens concatenated with the query embedding.
